headlines.article_text: Nvidia announces Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia's new DSX Pod AI Factory packages seven Vera Rubin AI racks in a shipping container designed to be transported by truck. All the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory. Nvidia did not disclose a price; analysts estimate a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., shows Vera Rubin computer modules during the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC in Berlin, Germany, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty Images Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing. The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said. "The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week. The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers. Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million. The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027. Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated. "What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up." Carlos Barria | Reuters OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies. For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers. Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models . Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks. "Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively. All three report quarterly results next week. Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model. OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering. Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface. Operating income in the connectivity unit about doubled to $2.37 billion. The AI business swung to a profit of $431 million, while the space division lost $7 million. Between infrastructure, cloud deals and paying users of the Grok AI models and products, Musk said on the call that annual recurring revenue by the end of next year will be between $500 billion and $1 trillion. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: SPCX, SMCI, NFLX & more Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket: Intuitive Surgical — The medical robotics stock slid 6% as the company's third-quarter results failed to impress investors. Intuitive Surgical earned $3 per share, excluding certain items, on revenue of $3.05 billion. SpaceX — Shares gained 8% after the Elon Musk-led rocket company reported a 161% jump in third-quarter revenue to $14.58 billion. Musk also said that SpaceX and Tesla , his auto manufacturer, have formed special committees to discuss a merger. Tesla shares were up 1%. Space stocks — Other aerospace companies were higher following SpaceX's earnings jump. Rocket Lab rose 2.5%, while AST SpaceMobile was higher by almost 3%. Firefly Aerospace jumped 3.5%. Netflix — Shares of Netflix fell almost 7% after the streaming giant reported third-quarter revenue that was in line with Wall Street's expectations. Sales came in at $12.87 billion, up 12% year over year, boosted by growth in membership and an increase in subscription prices that went into effect in March, the company said. AT & T — The telecommunications company slid 3.5% despite reporting an earnings and revenue beat in its third-quarter financial report. AT & T also hiked its full-year earnings guidance, though it reiterated capital expenditures that came in slightly above expectations, according to FactSet. Capital One Financial — The lender and credit card issuer gained 3% in premarket trading. Third-quarter net income reached $3.5 billion, or $5.61 per share, up from $3.2 billion, or $4.83 a share a year ago. United Airlines — The Chicago-based carrier fell 1% before the bell on Wednesday. Third-quarter adjusted EPS of $2.54 on revenue of $17.88 billion trailed Wall Street consensus estimates of $2.57 per share and $17.90 billion, according to LSEG data. Super Micro Computer — Shares rallied 12% after the data center server company hiked its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook. Super Micro sees revenue for the period between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, up from a previous range of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Dell Technologies , Hewlett Packard Enterprise — Super Micro's server competitors Dell and HPE were also higher on the news of the company's guidance update. Dell was jumping by 5.5%, while HPE rose 4.5%. Danaher Corporation — Shares lost 5.5% after the life sciences and diagnostics innovator reported a slight revenue miss in its third-quarter earnings report. Revenue came in at $6.55 billion, compared to analysts polled by FactSet's expectation for $6.56 billion. Adjusted earnings, however, beat estimates, and the company raised its full-year guidance for the metric. Philip Morris International — The tobacco and consumer goods company slipped 3% after it reported better-than-expected results in its third-quarter earnings report. However, full-year 2026 earnings guidance came in below expectations, according to analysts polled by FactSet. CME Group — Shares fell 1% despite the exchange reporting better-than-expected results in its third-quarter earnings report. CME delivered adjusted earnings of $3.02 per share, compared to a FactSet forecast of $2.99 per share. Revenue also came in slightly above estimates, as did operating income. — CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Fred Imbert and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting.
